source: seed (original guesstimate written for this app)
title: Cups of chai sold daily at Bengaluru City railway station
opening: How many cups of tea are sold in a day at Bengaluru City railway station (Majestic)?
client_context: A chai-vending startup is considering bidding for stall space at the station.
objective: Estimate daily cups of tea sold at the station, with a clear, defensible logic.

clarifications.answer: All tea sold within the station premises (platforms, concourse, stalls, and vendors on the platforms). Excludes shops outside the station.
A chai startup wants to know if a stall there would be worth bidding for.
Any hot tea, including cutting chai, regular chai and packaged tea sold in cups.

data.label: Footfall hint (only if the candidate asks for data)
data.content: We don't have exact figures. Assume what you think is reasonable, and tell me why.
data.release_when: Candidate asks for footfall or passenger numbers.

analytical_paths: Demand-side: daily footfall (passengers boarding/alighting + people accompanying + staff) × share who buy tea × cups per buyer, segmented by time of day/long-distance vs suburban.
Supply-side: number of stalls/vendors × cups per stall per hour × operating hours, with peak and off-peak.
key_insights: Segment users (long-distance passengers with waiting time vs short-hop commuters vs staff and vendors).
Supply-side cross-check (stalls × throughput) is the natural sanity check.
reference_solution: Demand: ~2 lakh people/day pass through (passengers ~1.5 lakh + companions/staff ~0.5 lakh). Long-distance passengers (~40%) have waiting time: ~35% buy, 1.2 cups each → ~25k cups. Short-hop commuters (~45%): ~10% buy → ~7k. Companions/staff/porters (~15%): ~40% buy, 1.5 cups → ~18k. Total ≈ 50k cups/day. Supply check: ~25 stalls + ~40 platform vendors; stalls ~120 cups/hour at peak for 6 hours and ~40/hour for 12 hours → ~1,200 cups/stall/day → 30k; vendors ~400/day each → 16k; ≈ 46k. Reasonable range: 30-70k cups/day.
alternative_approaches: Supply-side-only estimate with explicit stall throughput.
Train-based: number of trains × passengers per train × purchase rate.
recommendation: About 45-55k cups a day. For the startup: at ~₹15/cup that's a ₹7-8 lakh/day market at the station, so a single stall with ~3-5% share would sell ~1,500-2,500 cups a day, which helps evaluate the stall bid.
interviewer_notes: Evaluate logic, segmentation and sanity check, not the final number.
If the candidate asks for footfall, ask them to assume and justify it.
common_pitfalls: No segmentation (applying one purchase rate to everyone).
learning_objective: Demand-side decomposition with meaningful segmentation, cross-checked from the supply side.

title: Market size of home air purifiers in Delhi NCR
opening: Estimate the annual market size, in rupees, for home air purifiers in Delhi NCR.
client_context: A consumer-durables company is deciding whether to launch an air purifier range.
objective: Estimate annual market value for home air purifiers (new units sold plus filter replacements) in Delhi NCR.

clarifications.answer: Households only (not offices or hospitals). Include both new purifier sales and replacement filters.
Delhi NCR: Delhi, Gurugram, Noida, Ghaziabad and Faridabad.
Annual, in rupees, for the current year.

analytical_paths: Households → income segmentation → penetration → units in base → new sales (first-time + replacement units) and filter sales → multiply by prices.
Supply-side: brands/retail channels × units, as a cross-check.
key_insights: Segment by income: purchase is concentrated in the top ~20% of households.
Recurring filter revenue is a significant part of the market.
reference_solution: NCR population ~3.3 cr → ~75 lakh households. Affluent (can afford ₹10k+ purifiers) ~20% = 15 lakh; upper-middle ~25% = 19 lakh. Penetration: affluent ~35% (5.2 lakh HH, ~1.5 units each ≈ 8 lakh units), upper-middle ~8% (1.5 lakh units). Installed base ≈ 9.5 lakh units. Annual new sales: growth ~15% of base + replacement (5-year life, ~20%) → ~3.3 lakh units × ₹14k ≈ ₹460 cr. Filters: ~1 per unit per year × ₹3k × 9.5 lakh ≈ ₹285 cr. Total ≈ ₹700-800 cr.
alternative_approaches: Estimate via retail sales (stores × units per store per season) and online share.
recommendation: About ₹700-800 crore a year, roughly 60% hardware and 40% filters. The recurring filter revenue and the concentration in affluent households matter for the launch plan.
interviewer_notes: Check that the candidate includes filters and replacement demand, and sanity-checks penetration.
common_pitfalls: No sanity check on per-household spend.
learning_objective: Market sizing with income segmentation, installed base vs annual sales, and recurring revenue.

title: Public EV charging points needed in Bengaluru by 2030
opening: How many public EV charging points will Bengaluru need by 2030?
client_context: A charge-point operator is planning its city roll-out.
objective: Estimate the number of public charging points (not home chargers) needed in 2030.

clarifications.answer: Public charging points (a point = one connector that can charge one vehicle at a time), for cars, two-wheelers, three-wheelers and cabs. Home and captive fleet depots are excluded.
Assume a mix of fast DC chargers for cars/cabs and slower AC/swap points for two-wheelers. You can simplify.

analytical_paths: Vehicle parc in 2030 by segment × EV share × share relying on public charging × daily energy need ÷ energy one charging point can deliver per day at realistic utilisation.
Benchmark approach: EVs per public charger ratios in comparable cities, adjusted.
key_insights: Segmenting by vehicle type matters: cabs and three-wheelers depend on public charging far more than private cars.
Charger utilisation (not 24x7 at 100%) drives the answer.
reference_solution: 2030 parc: two-wheelers ~90 lakh, cars ~30 lakh, cabs ~2 lakh, 3W ~2 lakh. EV share: 2W 30% (27 lakh), cars 15% (4.5 lakh), cabs 60% (1.2 lakh), 3W 70% (1.4 lakh). Public dependence: 2W 15% → 4 lakh, cars 25% → 1.1 lakh, cabs 80% → ~1 lakh, 3W 60% → 0.85 lakh. Daily energy: 2W 2 kWh, cars 8, cabs 30, 3W 8. Daily energy totals: 2W 4 lakh × 2 = 0.8 GWh; cars 1.1 lakh × 8 = 0.9 GWh; cabs 1 lakh × 30 = 3.0 GWh; 3W 0.85 lakh × 8 = 0.7 GWh → ~5.4 GWh/day. Per point: fast DC 30 kW × 8 effective hours ≈ 240 kWh/day; AC 7 kW × 8 h ≈ 56. Cars/cabs/3W on DC: 4.6 GWh ÷ 240 ≈ 19k; 2W on AC: 0.8 GWh ÷ 56 ≈ 14k. Total ≈ 30-35k points.
alternative_approaches: Benchmark ratio method (e.g., ~1 public point per 10-15 EVs globally, adjusted for home-charging availability).
Location-based: charging hubs per km² in dense zones plus highway/corridor points.
recommendation: Roughly 30-35k public charging points, dominated by fast chargers for cabs and commercial vehicles. The operator should prioritise cab/3W-heavy hubs over residential car charging.
interviewer_notes: Probe the utilisation assumption; many candidates assume 24 hours of use.
common_pitfalls: Mixing up chargers and charging stations.
learning_objective: Multi-segment estimation driven by energy demand and capacity utilisation.

title: Wedding photography market in India
opening: What is the annual market size for wedding photography and videography in India?
client_context: A startup is building a marketplace for wedding photographers.
objective: Estimate annual spending on wedding photography/videography in India.

clarifications.answer: Professional photography and videography for weddings and pre-wedding shoots, paid to photographers or studios.

analytical_paths: Weddings per year (population → marriageable-age cohort, or marriages per 1,000 people) × segmentation by budget tier × share hiring professionals × average spend per tier.
Supply-side: number of professional photographers × weddings per year × average ticket.
key_insights: Budget-tier segmentation drives the answer: premium weddings are few but high-value.
Number of weddings can be derived from the population's age structure.
reference_solution: ~1 crore weddings a year (≈140 cr population; ~2.3 cr people turn 25 each year → ~1.1 cr couples). Tiers: premium 5% (5 lakh × ₹4 lakh = ₹20,000 cr); mid 25% (25 lakh × ₹1.2 lakh = ₹30,000 cr); budget 50% (50 lakh × ₹30k = ₹15,000 cr); bottom 20% mostly no professional (≈0). Total ≈ ₹65,000 cr (~$8 bn). Range: ₹40-90k cr.
alternative_approaches: Supply-side estimate from photographers × weddings × ticket.
Wedding industry size × share spent on photography (~8-10%).
recommendation: Around ₹60-70k crore a year, heavily skewed to the mid and premium tiers. For a marketplace, the mid-tier (25 lakh weddings, ~₹1.2 lakh each) is the core opportunity.
interviewer_notes: Ask how they got the number of weddings, and for a sanity check against the size of the overall wedding industry.
common_pitfalls: Using an unjustified number of weddings.
Single average spend with no tiers.

title: Daily revenue of a premium café in Indiranagar
opening: Estimate the daily revenue of a premium coffee chain outlet on 100 Feet Road, Indiranagar, Bengaluru.
client_context: A landlord wants to estimate what rent the outlet can afford.

clarifications.answer: About 60 seats, open 8 am to 11 pm, with dine-in, takeaway and delivery apps.
An average day across the week.

analytical_paths: Supply-side: seats × occupancy by time band × turns per hour × average bill per seat, plus takeaway and delivery.
Demand-side: footfall past the outlet × conversion × average bill.
key_insights: Time-of-day segmentation (morning, lunch, evening peak, late) is essential.
reference_solution: Dine-in: 60 seats; morning (8-11) 30% occupancy, ~1 turn/hr → 54 covers; midday (11-4) 50%, 0.8 turn/hr → 120; evening (4-9) 80%, 1 turn/hr → 240; late (9-11) 50%, 0.7 turn/hr → 42. ≈ 450 covers × ₹350 ≈ ₹1.6 lakh. Takeaway + delivery ≈ 35% of dine-in ≈ ₹55k. Total ≈ ₹2.1 lakh/day (~₹7.5 cr/yr). Range ₹1.2-3 lakh/day.
alternative_approaches: Barista throughput as a supply cap (orders per hour at peak).
recommendation: About ₹2 lakh a day (~₹7-8 crore a year). With rent typically 10-15% of revenue, the outlet could afford roughly ₹6-9 lakh a month.
interviewer_notes: Ask for a sanity check against throughput at peak (can baristas make that many drinks?).

title: UPI payments received by kirana stores in a day (India)
opening: Estimate the number of UPI transactions received by kirana stores across India in a day.
client_context: A fintech wants to size a lending product based on kirana UPI flows.
objective: Estimate daily UPI transactions at kirana (neighbourhood grocery) stores in India.

clarifications.answer: Kirana stores, meaning small independent grocery and general stores. Customer-to-merchant UPI payments only.

analytical_paths: Supply-side: number of kiranas (urban/rural) × transactions per store per day × UPI share.
Demand-side: households × grocery trips per day × UPI share.
key_insights: Urban vs rural split drives UPI share.
Cross-check against total national UPI volume (a sanity check that caps the answer).
reference_solution: ~1.2 crore kiranas: urban 35 lakh, rural 85 lakh. Urban: ~150 bills/day, 55% UPI → ~82 → ~29 cr. Rural: ~60 bills/day, 25% UPI → 15 → ~13 cr. Total ≈ 40 cr UPI transactions/day. Sanity check: total UPI in India is ~60+ cr/day, of which person-to-merchant is ~60%; kiranas at ~40 cr would be most of P2M, so it may be high → adjust to ~20-30 cr.
alternative_approaches: Demand-side from households × daily grocery purchases × UPI share.
recommendation: Roughly 20-30 crore UPI transactions a day, triangulated against national UPI volumes. For the lender, urban kiranas generate most of the flow.
interviewer_notes: Great candidates sanity-check against total national UPI volume and revise.
learning_objective: Bottom-up estimate with a top-down sanity check and willingness to revise.
